clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive type II congenital disorder of glycosylation caused by biallelic SLC39A8 variants, which encode the divalent metal transporter ZIP8 that supplies manganese and zinc to cells.

Manganese is an obligate cofactor for several Golgi glycosyltransferases, notably beta-1,4-galactosyltransferase, so cellular manganese deficiency drives a secondary defect of galactosylation and sialylation.
Severe infantile presentation with developmental delay, hypotonia, seizures, dystonia and cerebellar atrophy, sometimes with a Leigh-like picture.
Low whole-blood or serum manganese is a key diagnostic clue that distinguishes it from most other glycosylation disorders.
Cranial and skeletal features, short stature and sensorineural hearing loss may be present.
It is one of the rare treatable CDGs: oral galactose and carefully monitored manganese supplementation can improve glycosylation and clinical status in some patients.
Transferrin isoelectric focusing shows a type II pattern with loss of terminal galactose and sialic acid residues.
reference.pathophysiology: SLC39A8 encodes ZIP8 (Zrt/Irt-like protein 8), a transmembrane transporter that mediates cellular uptake of manganese and zinc. Biallelic hypomorphic variants reduce intracellular manganese, and because manganese is the essential cofactor of several Golgi glycosyltransferases, in particular beta-1,4-galactosyltransferase and the enzymes adding terminal galactose and sialic acid, N- and O-glycan maturation fails and a type II pattern of hypoglycosylation results. Systemic manganese deficiency also impairs other manganese-dependent enzymes such as arginase and mitochondrial superoxide dismutase, and the combination of hypoglycosylation with broader manganese-dependent metabolic disturbance underlies the neurodevelopmental, cerebellar and skeletal phenotype; supplementation that restores intracellular manganese can partially correct the galactosylation defect.

additionalInvestigations: Serum and whole-blood manganese (typically low) and zinc
Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing / glycoform analysis (type II pattern)
Molecular testing of SLC39A8 with a CDG panel or exome sequencing
Brain MRI (cerebellar atrophy and, in some, Leigh-like changes)
Monitored trial of galactose and manganese supplementation with serial transferrin glycoform assessment
redFlags: Rapid neurological deterioration or Leigh-like metabolic decompensation
Refractory seizures in an infant with hypotonia and dystonia
Manganese supplementation given without monitoring, risking manganese neurotoxicity and overload
Progressive loss of motor and cerebellar function
reference.prognosis: The natural history is severe with substantial neurodisability, but a subset of patients show meaningful biochemical and clinical improvement with galactose and carefully monitored manganese supplementation, so early recognition is worthwhile.
pitfalls: Missing the low manganese because it is not part of routine metabolic panels.
Giving manganese supplementation without monitoring, risking manganese accumulation and toxicity.
Dismissing the type II transferrin pattern as non-specific and not pursuing the specific gene.
Confusing it with the SLC39A14 and SLC30A10 manganese-overload disorders, which require the opposite (chelation) approach.
